options.text: By converting all asynchronous calls into synchronous C functions
options.explanation: Swift test runners cooperate natively with Swift Concurrency without C bridges.

options.text: By running all tests in kernel space
options.explanation: Unit tests execute in standard user space.

options.text: By disabling the Swift runtime type checker

questions.prompt: Why was testing asynchronous code harder in older Objective-C and legacy Swift?

options.text: Because Xcode refused to compile test targets
options.explanation: Xcode has always supported unit test targets.

options.text: Because tests required manual XCTestExpectation setup and completion callbacks
options.explanation: Testing callbacks required creating expectations, fulfilling them in closures, and waiting with timeouts.

options.text: Because iPhones had single core processors
options.explanation: Multicore iOS devices have existed for many years.

options.text: Because unit tests only supported synchronous math equations
options.explanation: Asynchronous testing has been possible, but previously required expectation boilerplate.

questions.prompt: How do you test an actor-isolated method from a unit test?

options.text: By calling the method synchronously without keywords
options.explanation: Actor-isolated methods cannot be called synchronously from outside the actor.

options.text: By disabling the actor isolation checks in build settings
options.explanation: Swift 6 compiler enforces actor isolation unconditionally.

options.text: By subclassing the actor into a struct
options.explanation: Actors are reference types and do not support struct inheritance.

options.text: By calling the method asynchronously with the await keyword
options.explanation: External calls to actor methods are asynchronous and must be awaited.

questions.prompt: What happens when an async test function encounters an await expression?

options.text: The test suspends cooperatively without blocking thread execution until work finishes
options.explanation: await is a suspension point that allows the underlying thread to perform other work.

options.text: The test aborts and marks the test suite as failed
options.explanation: Suspension is normal execution, not a test failure.

options.text: The operating system restarts the test runner simulator
options.explanation: The test runner continues running smoothly.

options.text: The compiler transforms the test into a background daemon
options.explanation: The test remains a standard function executed by the runner.

questions.prompt: Which Swift keyword enables testing multiple concurrent async operations simultaneously in structured concurrency?

options.text: defer
options.explanation: defer schedules execution for when the current scope exits.

options.text: async let
options.explanation: async let starts child tasks concurrently and allows awaiting their combined results.

options.text: guard let
options.explanation: guard let unwraps optionals conditionally.

options.text: fallthrough
options.explanation: fallthrough transfers execution in switch statements.

questions.prompt: How can you test legacy callback-based functions using modern async/await in Swift?

options.text: By adding while loops that poll a global variable
options.explanation: Polling while loops waste CPU and lead to flaky tests.

options.text: By converting the callback closure into an Objective-C selector
options.explanation: Selectors do not convert callbacks to async/await.

options.text: By wrapping the callback with withCheckedContinuation or withCheckedThrowingContinuation
options.explanation: Continuations bridge legacy callback closures into modern async functions.

options.text: By terminating the application process on completion
options.explanation: Terminating the process crashes the test runner.

questions.prompt: Why is inserting Task.sleep into unit tests considered bad practice?

options.explanation: Task.sleep is not deprecated.

options.text: Because Task.sleep crashes the device simulator
options.explanation: Task.sleep executes normally in simulators.

options.text: Because Task.sleep can only be called from SwiftUI body properties
options.explanation: Task.sleep is a general concurrency API.

options.text: Because sleep delays make tests slow and lead to flaky, timing-dependent failures
options.explanation: Arbitrary delays waste time on CI and fail unpredictably when machine load varies.

options.text: dispatch_group_wait

options.text: #available

options.text: preconditionFailure

questions.prompt: What danger arises when launching an unawaited detached Task inside a test method?

options.text: The test runner deletes the Xcode test plan
options.explanation: The test plan is not modified by running code.

options.text: The test method exits and reports success before the background task completes, causing false passes
options.explanation: Unawaited tasks outlive the test method, masking assertion failures and crashes.

options.text: The compiler fails with a syntax error
options.explanation: Creating a detached task is valid syntax, but logically dangerous in tests.

options.text: The detached task executes on the GPU
options.explanation: Tasks execute on CPU cooperative thread pools.

questions.prompt: Why should expectation timeouts in automated test suites be kept short (e.g. 1 to 2 seconds)?

options.text: Because macOS cannot count past ten seconds
options.explanation: macOS timers support indefinite durations.

options.text: Because Apple forbids timeouts greater than two seconds in the App Store
options.explanation: Unit test targets are not submitted to the App Store.

options.text: To prevent broken or hanging tests from stalling continuous integration queues for minutes
options.explanation: Short timeouts provide fast feedback and avoid wasted CI pipeline minutes.

options.text: Because Swift 6 strictly limits test execution to one second
options.explanation: Swift 6 imposes no arbitrary 1-second timeout on tests.

questions.prompt: What problem occurs if multiple asynchronous tasks mutate shared test state without synchronization?

options.text: The compiler replaces the tests with stubs
options.explanation: The compiler does not replace test code.

options.text: The test runner prints a success notification immediately
options.explanation: Data races do not produce immediate success notifications.

options.text: The Xcode window closes automatically
options.explanation: Xcode does not close due to data races.

options.text: A data race occurs, causing random test crashes or Swift 6 compiler diagnostic errors
options.explanation: Shared mutable state across tasks violates Swift 6 strict concurrency rules.
